lesson.title: Watching the Network: How SNMP Lets Admins Monitor Everything at Once
lesson.summary: SNMP is a standardized protocol for monitoring and managing network devices from a central console, letting an administrator both poll devices for status information and receive immediate alerts when something goes wrong.
lesson.body:
A network of any real size includes routers, switches, servers, and printers scattered across buildings or data centers, and an administrator cannot practically walk up to each one to check whether it is healthy. SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol, exists to solve exactly this problem: it defines a standard way for a central management system to query and, when necessary, reconfigure devices scattered across a network, all using one common, vendor neutral protocol. That standardization, laid out in RFC documents, is what makes it possible for a single monitoring system to talk to routers, switches, and servers from entirely different manufacturers using the same protocol rather than needing custom software for each vendor's equipment.

An SNMP deployment has a few standard pieces. A network management station, sometimes just called the manager, is the central console an administrator uses. Each monitored device runs an agent, a small piece of software that exposes information about that device, such as interface traffic counters, CPU load, or error counts. What exactly can be read or changed on a given device is organized into a Management Information Base, or MIB, a structured, hierarchical catalog of manageable values, each identified by a dotted numeric address called an object identifier, or OID.

SNMP supports a small set of operations built around this manager and agent relationship. A GET lets the manager request the current value of a specific OID from an agent, and a GETNEXT lets it walk through a sequence of OIDs to explore what is available. A SET lets the manager change a configurable value on the device directly. These three are all initiated by the manager, meaning the manager has to ask before it learns anything, which works well for routine monitoring but is too slow for genuine emergencies. That is what the fourth operation, the TRAP, is for: an agent can send a trap to the manager on its own, the moment something notable happens, without waiting to be asked. Older versions of SNMP, particularly SNMPv1, authenticated requests using a community string, essentially a shared password sent along with every request in plaintext, which is weak by modern standards; SNMPv3 later added real authentication and encryption to address that weakness.

Consider a router being monitored by a network management station. The manager might poll the router's interface counters via SNMP GET every five minutes, tracking bytes in and bytes out over time to build a bandwidth usage graph, an entirely routine, scheduled check. Now suppose that same interface's physical link fails at some point between two of those scheduled polls. Rather than the outage sitting unnoticed for up to five minutes until the next poll happens to reveal it, the router's SNMP agent can send a trap to the manager the instant the link goes down, so the administrator finds out immediately rather than waiting on the polling schedule. This combination, routine polling for ongoing trends plus immediate traps for sudden events, is what makes SNMP effective for keeping an eye on a large network without staring at every device all the time.
